source.title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models
source.authors: Kiho Park; Yo Joong Choe; Victor Veitch

page_placements.theme: Linear concept decoding, vector relations and their limits

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies linear concept representations and their geometry, but does not test sparse feature superposition, capacity competition, SAE features, or which units are superposed.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results about concept directions in LLaMA-2 and Gemma, including alignment and orthogonality under different inner products. These concern linear concept representations, not the sparse-overcomplete features or capacity effects named in the claim versions; they are recorded under fits_no_version. Random word pairs are a reference comparison, not a test of superposition.
record.test_reason: The paper formalizes and tests the linear representation hypothesis (concept directions, causal inner product) in LLaMA-2 unembedding space. It does not test superposition: no sparse features outnumbering dimensions, no polysemanticity, no capacity competition, no SAE/dictionary features. It cites Toy Models of Superposition only as background for linear representations. Its finding that 26 of 27 concepts are direction-like bears loosely on V6, but it does not compare 1-D against multi-dimensional features of superposed units. It also does not examine whether directions are superposed, so it is not a test of V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors formalize linear representation in counterfactual terms for both unembedding and embedding spaces, prove the links to probing and steering, and introduce a causal inner product that unifies the two. LLaMA-2 experiments show concept directions, probing and steering effects, and the importance of the inner-product choice. The record omits the probing and intervention experiments, but these are not relevant to the superposition versions.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce or apply the Toy Models of Superposition method; it formalizes and tests linear concept representations using counterfactual word pairs and an estimated causal inner product.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported geometry depends on inner-product choice: causal and Euclidean inner products differ, particularly in the Gemma-2B comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: Counterfactual word-pair differences project strongly onto a common concept direction for 26 of 27 concepts in LLaMA-2-7B unembedding space. The exception is thing⇒part.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Many binary lexical concepts are represented approximately as single directions in LLM unembedding space (linear representation hypothesis).

fits_no_version.finding: Causally separable concepts are near-orthogonal under a Cov(γ)^-1 inner product, with block structure for related concepts. Euclidean geometry is near-orthogonal in LLaMA-2 but not in Gemma-2B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Orthogonality of concept directions in LLMs depends on the inner product chosen; Euclidean cosine is not reliably semantically meaningful.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235, 2024
record.problems: The paper reports qualitative descriptions of several plotted results without uncertainty estimates; its experiments use selected concepts and do not evaluate superposition or capacity pressure.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results were included: the probing and intervention experiments concern the paper's linear-representation formalizations, not any of the claim versions.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, no sparsity sweep, no feature/dimension ratio, no geometry of superposed features.
All: no neurons or polysemanticity analysed.
All: works only in the final embedding/unembedding spaces, with no neuron distribution analysis and no dictionary learning.
It does not test whether superposed units are 1-D versus multi-dimensional. Its concept-direction results concern hand-picked binary concepts in the unembedding space, not superposed features.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The probing (Fig 4, 10, 11) and intervention (Fig 5, 12; Tables 1, 5, 6) results are correctly left out as irrelevant to V1–V6. There is no verdict, since no version is tested.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether sparse features outnumber dimensions, overlap, or have a sparsity-dependent transition or regular geometry.
Does not test polysemanticity, feature competition for capacity, or dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity indicates superposition.
Does not measure feature distribution across neurons or recover sparse features with a dictionary or SAE.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Tests concept directions as linear representations, but does not test whether the units involved in superposition are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: llama-2-7b
rows.operation_detail: Compared projections of counterfactual word-pair differences onto estimated concept directions with projections of randomly sampled word-pair differences.
rows.measure: Alignment of counterfactual-pair differences with the estimated concept direction under the causal inner product, compared with random-pair differences.
rows.baseline: Differences between 100K randomly sampled word pairs, projected onto the estimated concept direction.
rows.value: For 26 of 27 concepts, counterfactual-pair differences were substantially more aligned with the estimated direction than random-pair differences; thing⇒part was the exception.
rows.note: The authors say the counterfactual differences point to a common direction up to noise; this is evidence about linear concept representations, not superposition.
rows.check: State should be observed: 26 of 27 concepts align with their estimated direction, and only thing⇒part fails. The row is a main result rather than a comparator; random pairs are its baseline. It is not linked to any version.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4, Figure 2 and accompanying paragraph; Appendix C; Appendix D.1, Figure 7.
source_check.problem: The comparator role is inaccurate: alignment is the main measured result; random-pair differences supply its baseline.

rows.subject: llama-2-7b
rows.operation_detail: Measured pairwise inner products of estimated concept directions under the estimated causal inner product.

conditions.value: estimated causal inner product based on Cov(γ)⁻¹

rows.measure: Pairwise inner products of estimated unembedding concept directions; expected to be near zero for causally separable concepts.
rows.value: Most pairs of concepts were nearly orthogonal, with a clear block-diagonal structure and some non-zero structure among semantically related concepts.
rows.note: The result concerns the geometry of the paper's selected concepts under its estimated causal inner product.

rows.subject: llama-2-7b
rows.operation_detail: Compared concept-direction cosine similarities under the estimated causal and Euclidean inner products.
rows.measure: Pairwise cosine similarities between estimated concept directions.
rows.value: The Euclidean inner product somewhat preserved orthogonality for most causally separable concepts, but the causal inner product improved on it; examples include frequent⇒infrequent and the language concepts.
rows.note: This compares geometric choices for concept representations; it does not measure superposition.
rows.check: This is a method comparison (causal vs Euclidean inner product), not a superposition measure. The LLaMA-2 Euclidean geometry was also near-orthogonal for most separable concepts.

rows.subject: Gemma-2B
rows.operation_detail: Compared concept-direction cosine similarities under the estimated causal and Euclidean inner products.
rows.measure: Pairwise cosine similarities between estimated concept directions.
rows.value: The causal inner product captured the reported semantic orthogonality, whereas the Euclidean inner product did not.
rows.note: The text gives a qualitative comparison, not a result about overcomplete sparse features.
rows.check: The stage is not stated; this is the Gemma-2B base model, per the Mesnard et al. citation. It is a method comparison only.
